analysis.one_liner: Forces for-profit colleges to rely less on federal student aid, including veterans' GI Bill benefits, to keep their federal funding.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on February 23, 2021 and never advanced; no vote was ever taken before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already says a for-profit college must get at least 10% of its money from outside the federal government to qualify for federal student aid. This bill would have raised that to 15% and — importantly — counted veterans' GI education benefits as federal money (their monthly housing stipend would still not count). The point was to stop for-profit schools from running almost entirely on federal student aid and veterans' benefits while taxpayers absorb the losses when students get poor training and default on their loans. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges would benefit if the schools had to earn more of their money from non-federal sources — schools that cannot attract paying or non-federal customers on their own would have to improve or lose access to federal aid, and fewer students would be enrolled in programs funded almost entirely by federal dollars. Veterans would benefit because GI education benefits would no longer be counted as private revenue, reducing the incentive to recruit service members and their families into expensive low-quality programs. Taxpayers benefit because when a for-profit school's students default or the school collapses, the federal government (and thus taxpayers) eats the loss; reducing dependence on federal funds reduces that exposure.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum share of revenue for-profit colleges must earn from non-federal sources from 10% to 15%, forcing them to depend less on federal student aid to stay eligible.

Counts GI education benefits as federal funds, closing a loophole that let for-profit schools treat veterans' education benefits as private revenue; the Post-9/11 monthly housing stipend is exempted so veterans keep that money.
Requires annual public reporting to Congress of the share of each for-profit college's revenue coming from federal education assistance funds, based on audited financial statements.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges would bear the cost: schools that derive more than 85% of revenue from federal aid would have to find other revenue or lose participation in federal student-aid programs, which for many is the bulk of their income. Some might close, leaving enrolled students to find new programs — a transition cost the bill does not address.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new enforcement agency and adds no new penalties on its own; it raises the revenue requirement and relies on existing processes, so schools that game the numbers or close abruptly could still leave students and taxpayers holding losses.

Requiring for-profit colleges to attract 15% of revenue from non-federal sources could force some to cut programs or raise non-federal prices, and counting most veterans' education benefits as federal money reduces an incentive those schools had to serve veterans — a tradeoff an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: nearly all of the revenue of for-profit colleges comes from federal student aid and veterans' benefits, so raising the non-federal share and counting GI benefits closes two of the biggest ways taxpayers and veterans fund schools with poor track records. The costs are modest but real: some schools that cannot diversify their revenue might close, which could strand enrolled students, and supporters had to acknowledge that counting veterans' benefits (outside the housing stipend) could make some schools less able to enroll veterans. The bill also does not by itself bar a bad actor — it raises the bar, but enforcement still depends on the Education Department. On balance, the protections for students, veterans, and taxpayers outweigh the disruption, but it was a targeted fix, not a comprehensive overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up or brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only recorded actions were its introduction on February 23, 2021 and its referral the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No committee markup, hearing vote, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the 117th Congress.
With the 117th Congress adjourned on January 3, 2023, the bill expired and would need to be reintroduced to be considered again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that draw most of their revenue from federal aid, including GI benefits, keep the current rules and their federal funding untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges relying on federal aid

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Proprietary school operators and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against legislation raising the 90/10 revenue requirement and counting GI Bill benefits as federal funds, which would cut directly into the federal money their business model depends on.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — Cohen plus three Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support recorded — and the bill died in a Democratic-chaired committee without reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill raises the share of revenue these schools must earn outside federal aid and starts counting veterans' GI education benefits as federal money, closing the loophole that let them count veterans toward the 90% limit. Schools that rely almost entirely on federal aid would need to find new revenue or lose access to federal student aid — the money that sustains the industry.

By tightening the rules for for-profit competitors, the bill makes it harder for schools with weak outcomes to compete for the same federal aid dollars and students. The effect is indirect; the bill imposes nothing on these institutions.
